prompt: A disk is losing 3.23 GiB/day of free space and the operational action threshold is 50 GiB free. Which Prometheus function is purpose-built to project when that threshold will be crossed, based on a trailing window of historical samples?
choices: rate()
histogram_quantile()
predict_linear()
increase()

prompt: A capacity forecast alert based on predict_linear() is set with `for: 1h` instead of firing instantly. Why?
choices: Prometheus requires all alert rules to wait at least one hour before firing
A single noisy sample can push the linear projection across the threshold briefly; requiring it to hold for an hour avoids a flapping, ignorable alert
predict_linear() takes up to an hour to compute its result
It reduces the cardinality of the resulting time series

prompt: In a monthly cost showback report broken down by the `Team` tag, 17% of spend shows up as "untagged." What is the correct FinOps priority here?
choices: Ignore it since 17% is a normal rounding error in any cloud bill
Immediately start right-sizing the largest tagged instances, since untagged spend can't be acted on anyway
Treat closing the untagged gap as high priority: it represents real, unaccountable spend, often orphaned resources nobody owns
Delete every untagged resource automatically without investigation

prompt: A nightly batch reconciliation job is stateless, checkpoints progress regularly, and can tolerate a worker disappearing mid-run. Which purchasing change is the best fit for cutting its cost, based on its risk tolerance?
choices: Move it to Spot Instances, since its interruption tolerance matches Spot's reclaim risk
Buy a 3-year All-Upfront Reserved Instance, since reservations always minimize cost
Move it to a larger On-Demand instance type to finish faster
Leave it on On-Demand, since batch jobs should never use Spot

prompt: A VerticalPodAutoscaler is deployed with `updateMode: "Off"`. What does this configuration actually do in a production cluster?
choices: It disables the VPA object entirely, so it collects no data
It automatically evicts and resizes pods immediately based on observed usage
It only produces usage-based recommendations via `kubectl describe vpa`, without ever modifying running pods
It pauses the HorizontalPodAutoscaler for the same target

prompt: A Deployment's pods request 2 vCPU each but a two-week VPA recommendation shows p95 usage around 320m. What is the direct consequence of leaving the request at 2 vCPU?
choices: No consequence, since `limits` are what actually constrains the container at runtime
The cluster autoscaler provisions far more node capacity than the workload needs, because the scheduler bin-packs against the requested reservation, not real usage
The pods will be OOMKilled because the request is too low
Prometheus will refuse to scrape metrics from an over-requested pod

prompt: An HPA has no `behavior` block and flaps between 4 and 12 replicas under spiky traffic. To fix this while still scaling up quickly when load genuinely increases, what should the `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` be set to, relative to `scaleUp`?
choices: Set much higher than scaleUp's, so scale-down only acts after load has stayed low for a sustained period, while scale-up can react immediately
Set to 0, same as scaleUp, so both directions react instantly
Set much lower than scaleUp's, so the HPA removes replicas before it ever adds them
stabilizationWindowSeconds only applies to scaleUp and has no effect under scaleDown

prompt: Why is the error-ratio-style query pattern (rate of failures divided by rate of total requests) relevant when deciding whether a capacity or cost problem is urgent, rather than just looking at a raw utilization percentage?
choices: It isn't relevant; capacity planning only ever uses raw percentages
Raw percentages don't tell you the trend or the time remaining; a rate-based, threshold-driven forecast (like predict_linear) converts a snapshot into an actionable deadline
Ratios are always more accurate than counters in Prometheus
Rate-based queries are only valid for HTTP metrics, never for disk or memory
